issues.legal_issue: A discrepancy in a police-station daily-diary entry and the timing of an initial report do not establish that the report was fabricated when the surrounding evidence supports its timing and the diary entry is unreliable.
material_facts: The injured man was taken first to a local hospital and then to another hospital, where he died; the eyewitness who accompanied him went to the police station and lodged the report after his death.
The special report reached the magistrate in time, and the inquest report referred to the report and its registration.

The original daily-diary entry was not produced; a photocopy was produced after the prosecution had closed its evidence, and the recording officer testified that the report was recorded before the diary entry and that the entry was based on the report.
issues.conclusion: The report was not shown to be delayed unreasonably or created after deliberation, and the disputed diary photocopy did not falsify it.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 154 and Chapter XII of the Code of Criminal Procedure, information disclosing a cognizable offence is reduced to writing and its substance entered in the prescribed record; the Punjab Police Rules supplement rather than override the Code. The truth of a report cannot in every case be tested by comparing it with a police-station daily-diary entry. No earlier case is relied on in the judgment.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_challenging_report_timing and (medical_care_preceded_report and external_records_support_report_timing) and diary_original_unproduced and diary_entry_based_on_report

predicates.criminal_appeal_challenging_report_timin: The proceeding is a criminal appeal in which the timing or authenticity of the initial police report is challenged.
predicates.medical_care_preceded_report: The informant accompanied the seriously injured person for medical care before going to the police station to report the incident.
predicates.external_records_support_report_timing: Independent procedural records support the stated timing and registration of the report.
predicates.diary_original_unproduced: The original police-station daily-diary record was not produced, and the disputed entry was supported only by a copy.
predicates.diary_entry_based_on_report: Evidence showed that the police-station daily-diary entry was made after, and on the basis of, the initial report.

issues.definition: When a criminal appeal challenges a report’s timing, medical care preceded the report, external records support its timing, the original diary record is absent, and evidence shows the diary entry followed the report, the report is not shown to have been created later than claimed.

issues.legal_issue: An irregularity in an investigation does not by itself invalidate a trial conducted on the resulting case.
material_facts: The challenge relied on a disputed daily-diary entry and an asserted failure to follow the required sequence for recording information and making a diary entry.
The court found the original diary entry had not been produced and the available copy did not establish that the initial report was fabricated.
issues.conclusion: Any defect or procedural irregularity in the investigation did not, by itself, vitiate or nullify the trial.
issues.legal_principle: The investigation and registration process is governed by Chapter XII of the Code of Criminal Procedure, including Section 154. The Punjab Police Rules guide police officers and supplement, but do not supplant or override, the Code. An investigative defect, even a serious one, does not by itself affect the competence or procedure of cognizance or trial. No earlier case is relied on in the judgment.

predicates.criminal_trial_based_on_investigation: The proceeding is a criminal trial based on a police investigation.
predicates.investigation_procedural_irregularity: A procedural defect or irregularity occurred during the investigation.

issues.definition: When a criminal trial is based on an investigation in which a procedural irregularity occurred, that irregularity alone does not invalidate the trial.

issues.legal_issue: Eyewitness presence is not made doubtful solely because witnesses did not attempt a rescue or could not accurately identify the location of each injury during a violent attack.
material_facts: Two witnesses were near the victim when the attack occurred, and one of them had accompanied the victim to hospital and lodged the initial report.
The assailants were armed with dangerous weapons, which could have deterred the witnesses from intervening.
The attack involved several assailants and multiple blows, and one witness did not accurately describe the location of the injuries.
issues.conclusion: The witnesses’ presence at the scene was not reasonably doubted on the grounds that they did not intervene or that one witness inaccurately described injury locations.
issues.legal_principle: A witness’s reaction to a dangerous event cannot be judged by a universal standard; armed assailants may deter a bystander from intervening. In a fast-moving attack, a witness need not be expected to describe the nature and location of every injury with photographic accuracy. No earlier case is relied on in the judgment.

predicates.criminal_appeal_challenging_eyewitness_c: The proceeding is a criminal appeal in which the credibility or presence of eyewitnesses is challenged.
predicates.witnesses_naturally_present: The witnesses had an ordinary reason to be at or near the scene when the incident occurred.
predicates.armed_attack_could_deter_intervention: The assailants’ weapons or conduct could reasonably have deterred a witness from trying to rescue the victim.
predicates.attack_was_fast_moving: The victim was subjected to a rapid, multiple-person attack in which movement and confusion could make precise injury-location recall difficult.

issues.definition: When eyewitnesses were naturally present during a dangerous or fast-moving attack, their presence is not rejected solely because they did not intervene or could not precisely locate each injury.

issues.legal_issue: A participant who acts in furtherance of a shared intention to murder may be liable for the murder even if that participant’s own injuries were not individually sufficient to cause death.
material_facts: The accused attacked the victim together after one accused called for the victim to be killed.
The appellant was armed with a cutting weapon and inflicted two injuries on the victim during the attack.
Medical evidence showed that a separate head injury inflicted by another assailant was sufficient to cause death in the ordinary course of nature.
issues.conclusion: The appellant shared the common intention to murder and was liable for murder with the other participant under the joint-liability principle; the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 302 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code, a participant may be vicariously liable for murder where the material shows that an act causing the murder was done in furtherance of the participants’ common intention. It is not necessary that each participant inflict a fatal injury, and the individual injuries inflicted by a participant need not themselves be sufficient to cause death. No earlier case is relied on in the judgment.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_joint_murder_conviction and participants_attacked_together and appellant_armed_with_deadly_weapon and appellant_inflicted_injuries and attack_furthered_shared_intention_to_kill

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_joint_murder_convic: The proceeding is a criminal appeal from a conviction for murder based on joint liability.
predicates.participants_attacked_together: Multiple participants jointly attacked the victim.
predicates.appellant_armed_with_deadly_weapon: The appellant was armed with a weapon capable of causing serious or fatal injury.
predicates.appellant_inflicted_injuries: The appellant personally inflicted injuries on the victim during the attack.
predicates.attack_furthered_shared_intention_to_kil: The participants’ conduct during the attack showed that it furthered a shared intention to kill the victim.

issues.definition: When participants attack together in furtherance of a shared intention to kill, a participant who is armed with a deadly weapon and inflicts injuries may be liable for the murder even if another participant inflicted the fatal injury.
